key_points.point: The authors propose using LLMs to create an annotated database of state statutes, which serves the accelerationist goal of leveraging AI to solve complex information problems. By automating the analysis of millions of legal documents, this project demonstrates how AI can turn expert-level legal research into a scalable, accessible resource. This aligns with the accelerationist value of using AI to unlock new ways to conduct research and drive societal progress. The document acknowledges that this is an in-progress effort, noting that they currently face contractual limitations in making the full database available.
key_points.verbatim: We plan to use large language models (LLMs) to produce an annotated database of state statutes. This database would contain an easily accessible version of all state statutes and, within them, statutory clauses of interest to academics.

key_points.point: The project demonstrates AI's ability to tackle massive information problems that were previously impossible for humans to manage manually. The authors note that the aggregate of state law is so voluminous that traditional manual annotation is infeasible, making AI the only viable path for this research. This supports the accelerationist view that AI is the key to unlocking expert-level knowledge at scale. The document notes that their current collection for 2021 contains approximately 21 million sentences, illustrating the scale of the task.
key_points.verbatim: Because the aggregate of state law is so voluminous, the traditional approach of manual annotation is infeasible. Thus, we propose utilizing large language models to significantly automate the coding process.

key_points.point: The authors argue for using LLMs to semi-automate the coding of legal text, which aligns with the accelerationist method of using AI to augment research capabilities. By configuring LLMs to perform labeling with minimal manual input, they demonstrate how AI can be used to process vast amounts of complex data efficiently. This method allows researchers to annotate more variables than would be possible manually, accelerating the pace of empirical legal studies. The authors acknowledge that this methodology requires validation to ensure accuracy.
key_points.verbatim: We believe that modern machine learning techniques (namely, large language models) can be used to semi-automate annotation cheaply and accurately. LLMs can be configured to perform labeling using precisely the type of guidance given to a law student research assistant.

key_points.point: The project aims to create an open and accessible database of state statutes, which functions as a public utility for researchers. By making this data available, the authors hope to spur empirical research across disciplines, preventing the gatekeeping of legal knowledge. This aligns with the accelerationist goal of making powerful tools and data open-source and accessible to everyone. The authors hope this database will emulate other successful open-data projects like the Comparative Constitutions Project.
key_points.verbatim: Our plan is for the Stanford Neukom Rule of Law Center to publish and host the database with the hope of supporting empirical work on state law. Such a database would hopefully emulate what similar projects have done in other areas, including the Comparative Constitutions Project.

key_points.point: The authors report that modern LLMs are already capable of annotating legal texts with high accuracy, proving that scaling compute and model design leads to better performance on complex tasks. They cite an accuracy rate of over 90% for classifying private rights of action. This supports the accelerationist belief that current AI architectures are sufficient to achieve advanced intelligence with more resources and better training. The authors note that they intend to refine these methods further.
key_points.verbatim: For instance, researchers building from our efforts have identified at least twelve different LLMs capable of classifying private rights of action in statutory text at an accuracy rate greater than ninety percent.

key_points.point: The authors advocate for a collaborative, open-participation model for building the database, where the broader legal community contributes to defining variables. This mirrors the accelerationist argument that community-driven development is more effective for ensuring AI utility and safety. By integrating diverse subject-matter expertise, the project aims to create a more robust and useful tool for everyone. The authors acknowledge that this requires careful quality control.
key_points.verbatim: We hope to incorporate multiple researchers into the process of building this database and would like to invite other scholars to participate in the project by identifying variables that the database should include.

key_points.point: The project is designed to help solve the 'impossible' problem of tracking trends in state law, which is currently a bottleneck for legal research. By using AI to flag trends and provide granular data, the authors are using technology to solve a major societal challenge. This aligns with the accelerationist view that AI is the fastest way to build a better future by addressing complex global or societal problems. The authors note that current databases are simply not optimized for this type of research.
key_points.verbatim: Current databases do not provide granular data on statutory provisions, fail to flag trends in the adoption of new statutes across the states, cannot give fine-grained numbers on how many statutory provisions of a certain type exist, and are simply not optimized for cross-state statutory research.

key_points.point: The authors describe how they 'teach' the LLM to code statutes using descriptions and examples, which acts like a coach for the model. This transforms the AI from a passive database into an active assistant capable of performing complex legal reasoning. This supports the accelerationist view that special training methods are the key to turning raw information into real-world skills. The authors note that this process is much cheaper than manual annotation.
key_points.verbatim: LLMs can be “taught” to label text with only a description of the variable to be coded and a handful of examples. This makes them particularly useful for projects like ours, where the objective is to annotate many different variables with as little manual coding as possible.

key_points.point: The authors propose a transparent, auditable process where the AI's work is verified through validation samples. key_points.verbatim: We will work with participating scholars through the various stages of quality control to ensure that annotations are sufficiently accurate.

factual_claims.claim: Texas Senate Bill 8 allowed private parties to sue abortion providers to bypass federal court challenges.
Montana Senate Bill 419 imposed a $10,000 penalty for each violation of a TikTok ban.
States have added private remedies for harms arising from digital technologies like privacy and broadband accessibility.
The 2021 collection of state statutes contains approximately 21 million sentences and 440 million words.
Twelve different LLMs can classify private rights of action in statutory text with over 90% accuracy.
There are over 3,500 private-rights-of-action provisions in state law.

factual_claims.claim: There are 553 distinct statutory sections across 50 states tasked with promoting economic interests abroad.
There are 78 distinct enactments across 36 states preventing public entities from contracting with companies boycotting certain countries.
There are 64 distinct enactments across 43 states limiting the enforcement of foreign laws or judgments.
